newsitem.title: USA: Dollar closes on firm note in U.S. as stocks soar.
newsitem.headline: Dollar closes on firm note in U.S. as stocks soar.

text.p: The dollar ended higher but failed to recapture its sharp overnight gains after monetary officials in Japan and Germany raised the prospect of market intervention to slow the dollar's recent rally, traders said.

The two statements, made as the dollar climbed to a 34 month peak at 1.6935 marks and neared a four-high at 124.48 yen early Wednesday, quickly dropped dollar/mark by nearly two pfennigs, but the pullback was smaller against the yen, which held much of its gain into the U.S. close.
"As soon as the situation settled down people went right back to buying dollars," said Ben Strauss at Bank Julius Baer.
But the near-daily whispers of intervention will certainly temper dollar bullishness in coming sessions, added Strauss, assistant vice president at Julius Baer.
"Those statements ... spooked the market. The intervention threat does overhang the market," said Strauss.
The dollar ended higher at 1.6890/95 marks from 1.6829/34 at the open and 124.20/30 yen, up from 123.85/90.

During Asia trade, Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told a news conference the world's central banks would watch the markets carefully and "take appropriate measures to tackle any excessive moves."

Later, Bundesbank spokesman Manfred Koerber chimed in, reiterating the central bank's support for the G7 statement that currency misalignments had been corrected. He noted the G7 statement was made when dollar/mark stood at roughly 1.65.

While traders expressed doubt that the G7 would intervene at current levels, they said the mere possibility of official dollar selling convinced many investors to unload dollars and book profits from the current rally.
The dollar had rallied in early trading on the back of a New York Times article citing American exporters' relative comfort with a rally that has rocketed the greenback higher.
Since December 31, dollar/mark has risen 9.5 percent and dollar/yen 7.2 percent.
A strong dollar makes U.S. exports more expensive on world markets, but American firms have eased the impact by cutting costs and shifting production overseas, the article stated.
"That was very supportive for the dollar. Those companies are not complaining like they did during the dollar rally of the 1980s," said Francois Akl, chief currency dealer at Gulf International Bank.
In late New York trade the dollar got a boost from U.S. stocks, as the Dow Jones industrials finished up 103 points.
Barring actual G7 dollar sales, which dealers consider highly unlikely, investors will likely keep pushing the dollar higher in coming sessions, with a target range seen at 1.70 to 1.75 marks.

Solid U.S. economic growth, which contrasts with Japan's slumping economy and record German unemployment, continues to draw investors to U.S. stocks and bonds, which could bolster the dollar indefinitely.
"We have not yet reached a significant high, though the market can't just snub the central banks," said Marc Chandler, senior foreign exchange analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
In other trade, the dollar climbed to 1.4530/40 Swiss francs, a 34-month high, from 1.4425/35 at the open. The British pound was little changed at $1.6308/18 from $1.6310/20.
The dollar ended nearly flat at Canadian $1.3550/60 from C$1.3554/49. The Australian dollar rose to $0.7608/13 from $0.7565/70.
(( --Chris Stetkiewicz, 212-859-1664 ))
